claim: Apple's Q3 FY2026 company gross margin of 50.1% included an approximately 2-percentage-point favorable impact from tariff refunds; excluding this benefit, gross margin would have been at the midpoint of the prior quarter's guidance.
stance_target: Underlying (ex-refund) margin trend is flatter/weaker than the headline 50.1% suggests
scope_conditions: Apple fiscal Q3 2026 (June quarter), reported July 30, 2026
quoted_support: Company gross margin was 50.1%, up 80 basis points sequentially. This included a benefit from tariff refunds, which had a favorable impact of approximately two percentage points. When you remove this favorable impact, we would have been at the midpoint of the guidance provided last quarter.

claim: Apple's diluted EPS of $2.02 in Q3 FY2026 included $0.11 of favorable impact from tariff refunds, and products gross margin's 140bps sequential increase included over 2.5 percentage points of tariff-refund benefit.
stance_target: Headline EPS/margin growth is partly a non-recurring tariff-refund artifact
quoted_support: Diluted earnings per share was $2.02, up 29% year-over-year, and included 11 cents of favorable impact from tariff refunds. ... Products gross margin was 40.1%, up 140 basis points sequentially. This also included a benefit from the tariff refunds I just mentioned, which had a favorable impact of over 2.5 percentage points.

claim: Apple's Q4 FY2026 (September quarter) gross-margin guidance of 47-48% includes an expected ~1-percentage-point benefit from tariff refunds, a smaller benefit than the ~2pp realized in Q3 -- the refund tailwind is shrinking quarter over quarter.
stance_target: Tariff refund benefit is a decaying, non-recurring item rather than a structural margin improvement
scope_conditions: Guidance given July 30, 2026 for Apple fiscal Q4 2026
quoted_support: We expect gross margin to be between 47 percent and 48 percent. This includes an expected benefit of approximately one percentage point related to tariff refunds.

claim: Excluding tariff refunds, Apple's gross margin sequence was 48.0% in Q3 FY2026 falling to a 46.5% ex-refund midpoint guided for Q4 FY2026, and 'more than 100%' of both sequential declines is explained by rising memory (DRAM) costs, partially offset by carry-in inventory, lower non-memory component costs, and favorable mix.
stance_target: Apple's underlying margin trend is contraction (from memory-cost inflation), not the expansion implied by headline gross margin
quoted_support: if I look at the gross margin, you delivered 48% in the quarter without the tariff refund benefit. You're guiding to like 46 and a half... [Parekh:] that hundred and twenty basis point change... more than 100% of that can be explained by the memory cost change... We are seeing the same dynamics when you go from the 48.1 that we printed in the June quarter to the 46.5 midpoint... more than that is explained by the change in memory costs.

claim: Tim Cook characterized the current memory (DRAM) pricing environment as a 'hundred-year flood' with exponential price increases, citing it as the reason Apple 'reluctantly' raised iPhone/Mac/iPad prices, and noted the DRAM market has only three suppliers.
stance_target: Memory-cost inflation is an acute, potentially structural cost headwind for Apple's hardware margins
quoted_support: we reluctantly raised prices, I would say. And we did it because we're in, what I would characterize as a hundred-year flood on the memory pricing with exponential increases in memory prices, and so that was the rationale for it.

claim: Apple CFO Kevan Parekh orally attributed part of the Services growth deceleration (16% in Q2 to 12% in Q3 FY2026) to App Store business-model changes in certain countries and a US court ruling on link-out transactions, alongside mobile-gaming headwinds and an F1-movie comp effect.
stance_target: Regulatory/court-mandated App Store changes are contributing to Services growth deceleration
quoted_support: We also had some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store. We did see some headwinds in mobile gaming, and then keep in mind, we also made some changes to the App Store business model in certain countries, and in the U.S., we do continue to operate under a court ruling impacting the link-out transactions. But we're pleased the Supreme Court will hear our appeal.

claim: Apple states it plans to reinvest tariff refunds received into US manufacturing as part of its $600 billion four-year US commitment, including a new multi-year Broadcom silicon agreement expected to exceed $30 billion -- Apple's largest-ever American Manufacturing Program commitment.
quoted_support: Last year, we made a $600 billion commitment to the U.S. over four years, and now, as we said before, we plan to reinvest the tariff refunds we've received into the U.S. ... The new, multi-year agreement with Broadcom... is expected to exceed $30 billion. This marks our largest-ever American Manufacturing Program commitment.

claim: Apple experienced significant supply constraints in Q3 FY2026 driven by advanced-node SoC availability (not memory), expected to worsen 'significantly' in Q4 FY2026 across iPhone, Mac, and iPad, described by Cook as a demand-forecasting miss rather than a supplier problem.
stance_target: Apple's near-term hardware revenue growth is capacity- rather than demand-constrained
quoted_support: the root cause of it is not a regular supply issue. It's a demand forecast issue, to be candid, where the iPhone and the Mac are both doing remarkably better than we thought they would do... we've been pulling supply ahead, and at some point there's a limit to that.
